title: Creatable-object party in both Schools; fallen-object the commoner Roman view
source_text: XXXIII. Etenim, quod est valde observandum, quemadmodum sunt inter Reformatos nonnulli, qui praedestinationis objectum esse putant simpliciter hominem creabilem, minime vero hominem consideratum ut jam condendum & lapsum, quique censent decreto praedestinationis antecedaneum non esse praevisionem lapsus & creationis ejus qui eligitur, sic eandem quoque sententiam tuentur in Ecclesia Romana non pauci, omnes illi, scilicet, qui creationem praedestinatorum, & permissionem lapsus eorum in peccatum, inter effectus praedestinationis locum habere existimant, quique contendunt creationem ipsam ingredi decretum praedestinationis, & esse medium ad finem illius consequendum isti fini a Deo praedestinante subordinatum. Quo de numero post Scotum, Pighium, Naclantum, Catharinum, supra docuimus esse Gulielmum Estium, Alphonsum Mendozam & Dominicum Bannes, ex cujus doctrina, loco supra citato, Deo praedestinanti objicitur homo duntaxat possibilis. Ac sicut in Schola Romana plurimi ab hac sententia recedunt, ita quoque illam damnat & improbat major pars Doctorum Scholae Reformatae. Et denique sicuti plures inter Reformatos objectum praedestinationis constituunt hominem lapsum, sic etiam in Schola Romana haec sententia communiter obtinet.
pass_a_gloss: For — what is greatly to be observed — just as among the Reformed there are some who think the object of predestination to be simply creatable man, not at all man considered as already to be created and fallen, and who judge that foresight of the fall and of the creation of him who is elected is not antecedent to the decree of predestination, so also not a few in the Roman Church defend the same opinion — namely all those who think creation of the predestined and permission of their fall into sin have place among the effects of predestination, and who contend that creation itself enters the decree of predestination and is a means subordinated by God predestining to that end for attaining it. Of which number after Scotus, Pighius, Naclantus, Catharinus, we have shown above to be Gulielmus Estius, Alphonsus Mendoza, and Dominicus Bannes, from whose doctrine, in the place cited above, only possible man is set before God predestining. And just as in the Roman School many withdraw from this opinion, so also the greater part of the Doctors of the Reformed School condemn and disapprove it. And finally just as more among the Reformed constitute the object of predestination as fallen man, so also in the Roman School this opinion commonly obtains.
pass_b_english: Creatable-object party: Reformed and Roman (Scotus, Pighius, Naclantus, Catharinus, Estius, Mendoza, Báñez).
For them: creation & fall-permission are effects; object = possible/creatable man.
Majority of each School rejects that party.
Fallen-object is the commoner Roman view — and the more common Reformed too.
